intro: The building blocks, before and alongside week 1. Every item: read it, **🔊 hear it**, **🔤 hear it spelled** letter by letter, then test yourself. Nouns always come **with their article**.

sections.title: Alphabet
sections.tip: 26 letters. The French **names** of the letters matter: you'll spell your name, your street and your email out loud at every *démarche administrative* — and it's a classic listening item. Watch the traps: **e / i**, **g / j**, **h** (*hache*), **w** (*double vé*), **y** (*i grec*).

items.note: gé — English speakers confuse it with J
hache — the letter is silent in words
ji — English speakers confuse it with G
u — the French u (lips round, tongue forward)

sections.title: Accents & signs
sections.tip: Accents are part of the spelling — **a missing accent is a spelling mistake** in the writing paper. When you spell aloud, name the accent: *« e accent aigu »*.

sections.title: Vowels & vowel sounds
sections.tip: 6 vowel **letters** (a e i o u y) but about 15 vowel **sounds**. French vowels are **pure**: one sound, no glide. Each card shows one sound and the ways it's spelled.

sections.title: Consonants
sections.tip: Most final consonants are **silent** (*petit, grand, vous*). Remember **CaReFuL**: final **c, r, f, l** are usually pronounced (*avec, pour, neuf, avril*) — except -er verbs (*parler*). And **-ent on plural verbs is silent**.

items.note: « k » before a, o, u — « s » before e, i, y
items.ex: le café, la ville, cinq, le cinéma

items.note: hard before a, o, u — « j » before e, i, y
items.ex: la gare, le goût, manger, la région

sections.title: Numbers
sections.tip: Learn **0–20** cold, then the tens. The hard part is **70–99**: *soixante-dix* (60+10), *quatre-vingts* (4×20), *quatre-vingt-dix* (4×20+10). Listening papers love prices, times, phone numbers and dates — practise hearing numbers **fast**.
rules: **et** in 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71: *vingt et un, soixante et onze* — but **not** in 81 and 91: *quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze*.
**quatre-vingts** and **deux cents** take an **s** only when nothing follows: *quatre-vingts* but *quatre-vingt-trois*; *deux cents* but *deux cent dix*.
**mille** never takes an s: *deux mille vingt-sept*.
Hyphens join words under 100 (*dix-sept, quatre-vingt-dix*). Since 1990 you may hyphenate every part (*deux-cent-dix*) — both are accepted.
Belgium & Switzerland say *septante* (70) and *nonante* (90) — recognise them; Canada and France use *soixante-dix / quatre-vingt-dix*.
Dates use **le premier** for the 1st, then plain numbers: *le premier mars, le deux mars, le 12 février*.
French phone numbers are read in **pairs**: 06 12 34 56 78 → *zéro six, douze, trente-quatre, cinquante-six, soixante-dix-huit*.

sections.title: Days of the week
sections.tip: Days are **masculine** and written **without a capital**. *Lundi* = on Monday (this one); **le lundi** = on Mondays (every). The week starts on **lundi**.

items.ex: Le dimanche, je suis de garde.

sections.title: Months & seasons
sections.tip: Months are **masculine**, **no capital**, and take **en**: *en février*. Seasons: *au printemps*, but *en été, en automne, en hiver*. Dates: **le 12 février 2027** (article + number + month).

sections.title: Le / la — masculine & feminine
sections.tip: Every French noun is **masculine** or **feminine** — even objects: *le livre* (m), *la table* (f). The gender decides the article (**le/la**, **un/une**), the adjectives (*petit/petite*) and the pronoun (*il/elle*). There's no logic to it you can rely on, so **always learn a noun with its article**: not *livre* but *le livre*. The good news: the **ending** of a noun often gives the gender away (see the lists below).
rules: **le** = the (masculine) · **la** = the (feminine) · **l'** before a vowel or silent h — *both* genders: *l'avion* (m), *l'école* (f) · **les** = the (plural, both genders).
**un** = a (masculine) · **une** = a (feminine) · **des** = some (plural). Tip: with *l'* and *les* you can't hear the gender — check it with *un/une*: *un avion*, *une école*.
**Some** (partitive): **du** (m) · **de la** (f) · **de l'** (vowel) · **des** (plural): *du pain, de la viande, de l'eau, des fruits*. After a negative → **de**: *je n'ai pas **de** pain*.
**à / de + le** fuse: *à + le = **au***, *à + les = **aux***, *de + le = **du***, *de + les = **des***. So: *au cinéma*, *à la plage*, *à l'hôpital*, *le prix du billet*.
**My / your / his** follow the **noun**, not the owner: *mon frère, **ma** sœur, mes parents*. Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel use **mon**: *mon amie, mon école* (easier to say).

**Adjectives agree** with the noun: add **-e** for feminine, **-s** for plural: *un petit appartement → une petite maison → des petites maisons*. The -e often makes the last consonant **heard**: *petit* [pə-ti] → *petite* [pə-tit].
Gender is grammar, not biology: *la personne* (even a man), *le bébé* (even a girl), *la victime*, *le mannequin*.

**For the TCF:** one wrong gender won't stop anyone understanding you, but dozens of them lower your grammar mark in writing. In **speaking, never stop to fix a gender** — keep going. Fix genders in writing, in the proofread.

sections.title: Word bank
sections.tip: Themed everyday words, each **with its article** and a gender badge (**m.** / **f.**). The themes match what the TCF talks about: travel, town, work, home, health, family, paperwork. Hear each word, spell it, then drill: **Listen & choose**, **Dictation**, **Meaning** and **Le or la?**
rules: Learn nouns **with the article**: *l'avion* is useless on its own — learn *un avion* (m).
**Canada:** breakfast is *le déjeuner*, lunch *le dîner*, dinner *le souper*. In France: *le petit-déjeuner, le déjeuner, le dîner*. Know both.
**Jobs:** no article after *être*: *Je suis infirmière* (not *une infirmière*). But *C'est une infirmière*.
**Countries:** *au* + masculine country (*au Canada, au Nigeria*), *en* + feminine (*en France, en Angleterre*), *aux* + plural (*aux États-Unis*).
